Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Time, the calendar & feasts · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

celebrate verb

a feast or a happy day

classical

Plin. Ep. 6.30.1: nātālēs tuōs … celebrāre
Cic. Arch. 13: fēstōs diēs lūdōrum celebrandōs
Traupman 291: nātālem Chrīstī diem celebrāre
Traupman 74, 288

celebrō, celebrāre, celebrāvī, celebrātum

verb, first conjugation, transitive

celebrate (a feast, a birthday)

Properly “to fill with people”, hence to keep a feast in company (Lewis & Short). It names what is celebrated: nātālem, diem fēstum, nūptiās celebrāre.

Examples

  • Lūcifer ambōrum nātālibus adfuit īdem: ūna celebrāta est per duo lība diēs

    the same morning star was there at both our births: one day was celebrated with two cakes (Ovid and his brother, born a year apart)Ov. Tr. 4.10.11–12

  • dēbēmus mehercule nātālēs tuōs perinde ac nostrōs celebrāre

    we really ought to celebrate your birthdays as we do our ownPlin. Ep. 6.30.1

  • licet enim sine luxuriā agere fēstum diem

    for one can keep a feast day without extravaganceSen. Ep. 18.4

Other words

  • agō, agere, ēgī, āctum — keep, celebrate (a feast day, a birthday)

    verb, third conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Sen. Ep. 18.4: agere fēstum diem; Hor. C. 4.11.14: Īdūs tibi sunt agendae; Cic. Verr. 2.4.107

    The plain word, with the day as its object.

  • agitō, agitāre, agitāvī, agitātum — keep, celebrate (a feast)

    verb, first conjugation, transitive · also used · classical · Ter. Heaut. 733: mīles Dionȳsia agitat; Gell. 18.2.1: Sāturnālia Athēnīs agitābāmus

See also festival, birthday, birthday party, anniversary.
